title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 1: Judicial Activism in the Philippines
keywords: Lopez v. Senate of the Philippines
to afflict the comfortable and to comfort the afflicted
Its might is in its being right
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's address articulating the Filipino perspective on judicial power, arguing that Section 1 of Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution makes activism a duty rather than a choice for every Philippine judge, because a power may be relinquished but a duty may never be evaded

A comparison of Philippine and American judicial activism: the Warren Court quartet that dismayed Eisenhower against the Frankfurter-Jackson school of restraint, and the textual difference that gives American magistrates the luxury of choosing a philosophy while Philippine judges must decide every legitimate issue of grave abuse

His working rule for the political-question defense: where the Constitution grants absolute discretion, the courts may not substitute their own standards of wisdom, but where it imposes conditions, limitations or restrictions, the courts may review whether those were observed -- illustrated by Francisco v. House of Representatives and Lopez v. Senate of the Philippines

The use of the expanded certiorari duty in economic governance -- Meralco rate increases, Manila Bay reclamation, NAIA Terminal III, poll computerization, online gambling -- and his answer to business critics that Philippine judges are duty-bound 'to afflict the comfortable and to comfort the afflicted'

The constitutional architecture that supports this role: fiscal autonomy, security of tenure and compensation, impeachment-only removal, administrative supervision of the lower courts, control of the bar, and rule-making power -- and his closing claim that the judiciary's weakness becomes its strength when it speaks through well-reasoned decisions
sub_topics: He opens by noting the honor of speaking alongside US Court of Appeals Justice Harris Hartz and Thai Justices Vichai Vivitasevi and Navarat Klinratana before a rare single gathering of all Philippine appellate jurists
He tells the Eisenhower anecdote -- asked in 1961 about his great mistakes, the former president snapped that there were two and they were still sitting on the Supreme Court
He identifies those mistakes as Earl Warren and William Brennan, who with Hugo Black and William Douglas formed a quartet that overhauled American jurisprudence and expanded civil rights

He recalls that Warren, first dismissed as a bluff without judicial experience, retired hailed as one of the greater Chief Justices for Brown, Terry and Miranda, alongside Mapp, Sullivan, Gideon and Baker v. Carr

He sets out the opposing camp: Frankfurter and Jackson lecturing on judicial restraint and warning against entering the political thicket, believing the Court existed to establish rules of law rather than to provide justice
He gives the activists' reply that the Harvard School was too mechanical, had excised all heart out of the law, and that the real threat came from justices abdicating their duty to protect the people

He quotes Section 1 of Article VIII and divides it into the ordinary power of judicial review and the extraordinary or expanded certiorari responsibility over grave abuse by any branch or instrumentality
He argues that because this intervention is framed as a duty, all judges are mandated to be activist, and that shirking it would repeat the judicial cop-outs of the martial law years
He cites Tañada v. Angara that when legislative action is seriously alleged to infringe the Constitution the question is judicial rather than political and the Court is bound to decide
He contrasts the American position, where judicial review was never expressly conferred but was established by Marshall in Marbury v. Madison and settled by popular acquiescence
He answers the recurring objection -- why unelected judges may reverse the elected -- with the point that the sovereign people mandated it in a Constitution the electorate overwhelmingly ratified
He warns against being beguiled by foreign jurisprudence, citing Garcia v. Comelec and Father Joaquin Bernas's line that the new Constitution cut the umbilical cord to American case law

He credits former Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion, author of the provision, with explaining that the expanded mandate was a product of the martial law experience, when the political-question defense left tyrannies unchecked and judicial hand-washing encouraged further violations

He supplies the classic definition of a political question from Tañada v. Cuenco -- a question of policy dependent on wisdom rather than legality -- and distinguishes those decided by the people themselves from those delegated to Congress and the Presidency

He states his own guiding rule distinguishing absolute discretion, which courts may not limit, from powers subject to constitutional conditions, whose observance courts may review as a legal rather than political question

He applies the rule to Francisco v. House of Representatives, where the Court stopped the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide under the one-year bar of Article XI, Section 3 (5), without indiscriminately turning political questions justiciable

He contrasts Lopez v. Senate of the Philippines, where the Court refused to nullify the 22-person Joint Committee canvassing the May 10, 2004 presidential votes, ruling narrowly so as not to prejudge an ongoing canvass

He addresses the jurisdictional dispute, citing the 10-3-1 vote in Santiago v. Guingona and its reiteration in Lopez that jurisdiction is determined by the allegations of the initiatory pleading, so a petition alleging prima facie infringements is dismissed on the merits rather than for want of jurisdiction

He lists the economic cases in which the Court struck down contracts for grave abuse, noting its insistence on transparent and evenhanded public bidding and its description of one contract as the grandmother of all scams

He acknowledges the media and business backlash, compares his critics to Eisenhower and the New Deal laissez-faire advocates, and invites them to read the Francisco opinions, including his own Separate Opinion

He traces the evolution of 'grave abuse of discretion' from the subjective Rule 65 formula of capricious and whimsical judgment to the broader test of any act contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence

He enumerates the guarantees of judicial independence -- fiscal autonomy with an irreducible appropriation, security of tenure and compensation to age 70, removal only by impeachment or by the Supreme Court, and inviolable constitutional powers

He enumerates the judiciary's added prerogatives: administrative supervision and training of judges through the Philippine Judicial Academy, the Chief Justice's chairmanship of the Judicial and Bar Council, control of bar admission, MCLE and the Integrated Bar, and rule-making power including rules protecting constitutional rights

He closes by conceding that the judiciary remains the weakest branch -- without purse, police, army or patronage -- yet insists that this weakness becomes strength through moral courage born of competence and unassailable integrity

stances.claim: The 1987 Constitution makes judicial activism a duty rather than a choice, because Section 1 of Article VIII imposes on all judges the obligation to determine grave abuse of discretion -- and a power can be relinquished while a duty cannot be evaded.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual reading pressed into a moral obligation, with the martial law judicial cop-outs held up as the alternative

stances.claim: Much American jurisprudence on judicial review does not apply here, because the express activist mandate has no counterpart in the US Constitution and Section 1 of Article VIII was born of the Philippines' own experience of dictatorship.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative contrast authenticated by the provision's author, Chief Justice Concepcion, and by Bernas's 'umbilical cord' image

stances.claim: Courts may not limit a department's exercise of absolute constitutional discretion, but where the Constitution attaches conditions, limitations or restrictions, reviewing their observance is a legal and not a political question.
stances.rhetorical_move: a personal decision rule stated flatly, then tested against a case where the Court intervened (Francisco) and one where it refused (Lopez)

stances.claim: A petition alleging serious prima facie infringements of the Constitution vests the Court with jurisdiction, which it does not lose by later finding the allegations unfounded; the proper disposition then is dismissal for failure to establish grave abuse.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural clarification against scholars urging instant dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, supported by the 10-3-1 vote in Santiago and its reiteration in Lopez

stances.claim: Striking down abusive government contracts serves rather than deters economic development, because the rule of law is an essential ingredient of good governance and public biddings must be transparent and evenhanded, whatever the business community's criticism.
stances.rhetorical_move: answering critics by naming their lineage (Eisenhower, the New Deal laissez-faire advocates) and restating the judge's mandate to afflict the comfortable

stances.claim: Though it commands neither purse nor sword and cannot enforce its own pronouncements, the judiciary's weakness becomes its strength when it speaks through well-reasoned decisions upholding the supremacy of the Constitution.
stances.rhetorical_move: paradox as peroration: might reframed as moral courage born of competence and integrity

notable_anecdotes: He retells how Eisenhower in 1961, asked by CBS producer Fred Friendly about his great mistakes, answered instantly that there were two and they were still sitting on the Supreme Court.

He recounts that Earl Warren, first derided by liberals as a bluff and a mediocre politician without judicial experience, was hailed at his retirement by those same critics as one of the greater US Chief Justices.

He notes that the forum itself was a rarity -- all the appellate jurists of the country, from the Supreme Court to the Court of Tax Appeals, gathered in one place, with panelists from the United States and Thailand.

He relays Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion's explanation that the expanded certiorari mandate he drafted was a product of the martial law years, when the dictatorship's political-question defense left repressions unchecked.

He recalls that the Court once openly called a government contract the grandmother of all scams, and that the rulings on Meralco, Manila Bay, NAIA Terminal III and poll computerization got the Court pulverized in the media.
He invites critics to read Francisco v. House of Representatives, listing the Separate Opinions of eight colleagues before adding, with a note of self-deprecation, his own.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' reproduced CJP's address on judicial activism, delivered to a rare assembly of all Philippine appellate jurists alongside an American and two Thai justices. He opened with Eisenhower's 1961 quip that his two great mistakes were still sitting on the Supreme Court, identified them as Earl Warren and William Brennan, and sketched the Warren Court's expansion of civil rights against the counsels of restraint from Felix Frankfurter and Robert Jackson, who accused the activists of entering the political thicket while the activists replied that the Harvard School had excised all heart out of the law. He then turned to the decisive textual difference: Section 1 of Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution not only grants ordinary judicial review but imposes on every judge the duty to determine whether any branch or instrumentality has gravely abused its discretion. Because that intervention is framed as a duty and not a mere power, he argued, Philippine judges are mandated to be activist and may not shirk, waver or equivocate, on pain of repeating the judicial cop-outs of martial law. He credited Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion, the provision's author, with tracing it to the dictatorship's use of the political-question defense, and warned, with Garcia v. Comelec and Father Bernas, against being beguiled by American jurisprudence written for a different constitutional setting. He then offered his own rule: courts may not limit a grant of absolute discretion, but where the Constitution imposes conditions, limitations or restrictions, their observance is a legal question -- as in Francisco v. House of Representatives, where the second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide fell to the one-year bar, and unlike Lopez v. Senate of the Philippines, where the Court declined to disturb the canvassing Joint Committee. On jurisdiction he cited Santiago v. Guingona and Lopez for the rule that the allegations of the petition confer it. He defended the Court's economic rulings on Meralco rates, Manila Bay reclamation, NAIA Terminal III, poll computerization and online gambling against business criticism, saying Philippine judges are duty-bound to afflict the comfortable and comfort the afflicted; traced the widening definition of grave abuse from Rule 65's capricious-and-whimsical formula to any act contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence; enumerated the guarantees of judicial independence and the Court's added prerogatives over the lower courts, the bar and the rules of procedure; and closed by arguing that the weakest branch, lacking purse and sword, finds its strength in moral courage, for its might is in its being right.
